pages.title: Test File Generator for QA - Exact Size, {{ .Facts.FormatCount }} Real Formats

pages.title: Test File Presets - Ready-Made Sets for QA Questions

pages.title: Documentation - Commands, Recipes, Manifest, Exit Codes

empty-and-minimal.question: Does a file that is valid and as small as the format allows get through?
empty-and-minimal.title: Empty and minimal
empty-and-minimal.pageTitle: Smallest Valid and Empty Test Files in Every Format
empty-and-minimal.description: The smallest valid file this tool writes in each of its {{ .Facts.FormatCount }} formats, plus an empty file where the format allows one, each with the reaction to expect.
catches: a valid file turned away for being too small, where the check counts bytes instead of reading them
an empty file that brings the reader down rather than being reported
a picture one pixel wide that divides by zero on the way to a thumbnail
storage that reads nought bytes as a failed upload and keeps retrying

details.formats: Which formats the set is built from. Leave it at `all` for every format this build has, or name the ones your system accepts.

filename-handling.question: Will my system store, show and give back a file name it did not expect?

filename-handling.pageTitle: Problematic File Names for Testing - Unicode and Length
filename-handling.description: Test files whose names break uploads and storage: other scripts and emoji, a right to left override, invisible characters, shell and SQL syntax, length limits.
catches: a name that looks like a different one on screen, in a log or in a list
a name cut, trimmed or rewritten between upload and storage
a length limit counted in characters where the storage counts bytes

picture-sizes.question: Does my system take pictures at the sizes screens and platforms use?
picture-sizes.title: Picture sizes
picture-sizes.pageTitle: Test Images at Common Sizes - Screens, Avatars, Social Media
picture-sizes.description: Pictures at the sizes of HD, Full HD, QHD and 4K screens, of profile pictures, and of the covers, posts and thumbnails social platforms ask for.
catches: a limit on the width or the height set with one shape in mind that turns away another, such as a profile background 1584 px wide
a thumbnail cut or squashed because the code expects a landscape picture and a portrait one arrives
a picture with an odd height, such as 1200 x 627, refused by a step that only takes even sizes
a 4K picture that runs out of time or memory on its way to a thumbnail, although the file itself is small

details.groups: Which sizes the set holds: `screens` for the sizes of screens, `avatars` for profile pictures and `social` for covers, banners, posts and thumbnails. Leave it at `all` for every one of them.
details.content: What the picture shows. A test pattern is for checking how a file is read. A placeholder is a flat colour with words in the middle, for laying out a page before the real pictures exist.

size-boundaries.question: Is a size limit enforced exactly where it is declared?
size-boundaries.title: Size boundaries
size-boundaries.pageTitle: Test an Upload Size Limit - Files at the Exact Boundary
size-boundaries.description: Files one byte under, at and one byte over the size limit your system declares, plus wider steps either side, each marked with whether it should be accepted.
catches: off by one errors at the limit
MB confused with MiB, which is 4.8 per cent and enough to let a file through that should not pass
a limit enforced in the browser and not on the server

details.limit: The size limit your system declares. Everything else is measured from it.
details.spread: How far either side of the limit to reach, as a list of sizes.

tabular-import.question: Does my table import survive what real tools export?
tabular-import.title: Tabular import
tabular-import.pageTitle: CSV and Excel Import Test Files - Delimiters, Headers
tabular-import.description: CSV files with other delimiters, CR LF endings, no header and other quoting, a table wider than a spreadsheet shows, an Excel workbook and JSON in several layouts.
catches: a semicolon file read as one column, because the delimiter was assumed rather than looked for
a CRLF file split into rows with an empty row after each one
a headerless table whose first row of data is eaten as column names
an import that keeps the columns it can show and drops the rest without a word
a reader that takes JSON records one line at a time and stops at the first indented document

details.rows: How many rows the spreadsheet holds. It is written at exactly the size that many rows package to, so the budget above moves with this.
details.columns: How many columns each row of the spreadsheet has. Rows times columns has a ceiling, and asking past it is refused before anything is written.

text-encoding.question: Does my reader know which encoding a file is in, or is it guessing?
text-encoding.title: Text encoding
text-encoding.pageTitle: Text Encoding Test Files - UTF-8, UTF-16, BOM, CRLF
text-encoding.description: The same text in UTF-8, UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE, with and without a byte order mark, and files ending lines in CR LF and LF, to test how a reader decodes text.
catches: a reader that assumes UTF-8 and shows a UTF-16 file as one character in three, or as rows of boxes
a byte order mark read as content, so the first field of an import starts with three stray characters
an importer that guesses the encoding from the opening bytes and guesses differently for a longer file
a CRLF file split into rows with an empty row after each one, or a carriage return kept inside the last field

details.sample: How big each file of the set is. UTF-16 stores two bytes for every character, so an odd number is refused.

upload-validation.question: Does my upload form take what it should and turn the rest away?
upload-validation.title: Upload validation
upload-validation.pageTitle: Upload Validation Test Files - Type, Size and Name
upload-validation.description: Files for testing an upload form: allowed and denied types, content that does not match its extension, the size limit either side, hostile names and a bulk upload.
catches: a limit enforced in the browser and not on the server
an SVG or an HTML file taken for a picture or for plain text, which is a way to get a script past a form
a file checked by its extension and never opened, so a PDF named .jpg goes through
a form that reads the whole body into memory before it looks at how big it is
an upload named PHOTO.JPG turned away where photo.jpg is taken, or the other way round
a name with spaces, brackets or characters outside ASCII written to disk unchanged
a name with a path in it, such as ../, used as given, so the file is written outside the upload directory

details.limit: The size limit your upload form declares. This set takes one step either side of it - for a file at every distance, run the size-boundaries preset.
details.allow: Which types your form is supposed to accept. Each one becomes a real file of that type, and they are the positive control of the whole set.
details.deny: Which extensions your form is supposed to turn away. An extension this build has no format for still gets a file under that name, holding plain text.
details.far-over: How far past the limit the one big file goes. Turn it off where writing several times the limit is not worth the disk.
details.bulk: How many files the mass upload holds. Nought leaves that group out of the set altogether.

faq.q: How is this different from dd, fsutil or truncate?
faq.a: Those give you a file of the right size full of nothing. A 2 MB file named photo.png made that way is not a PNG, so anything that really parses it rejects it for the wrong reason, and your test then passes for the wrong reason too. This produces a real PNG of exactly 2 MB that opens in an image viewer, and it arrives with a statement about how your system should treat it.

faq.q: Is it free, and can I use it at work?
faq.a: Yes to both. It is released under GPL-3.0 and costs nothing. There is no account, no licence key and no paid tier.

faq.q: Can I use the generated files in a closed source product?
faq.a: Yes. The licence covers the code of the tool, not what the tool produces. Generated files, recipes and manifests are output rather than derived works, so you can commit them and ship them with no obligation.

faq.q: Do the generated files contain real personal data?
faq.a: No. Everything inside is synthesised from a seed. No dataset is read, no service is contacted and no third party content is embedded. Treat a generated e-mail address as unusable rather than unused, because any random string can collide with a real one by chance.

faq.q: Will I get exactly the same files on another machine?
faq.a: Yes, byte for byte, given the same recipe and the same seed. The project tests that on every change, and breaking it requires a major version bump. That is what lets you commit a small recipe instead of large binary fixtures.

faq.q: Does it need an internet connection?
faq.a: Never. There is no telemetry, no update check and no cloud client, and the command line binary does not have a network stack compiled into it at all. It works on a machine with no network and inside a closed corporate environment.

faq.q: What happens if I ask for a size a format cannot reach?
faq.a: You get an error naming the format, the smallest it can be, the reason for that floor and what to do instead, and no file is written. The tool never rounds a size silently. Every floor is listed on the formats page.

faq.q: Can I generate a file that is deliberately broken?
faq.a: Yes. Add --damage zero-head and the file comes out at exactly the size you asked for with its first bytes overwritten by zeros, so a reader turns it away, and the manifest says your system should reject it. The page about corrupt test files has the details.
7z and mp3. {{ .Facts.FormatCount }} formats work end to end today.

faq.q: Which systems can I run it on?
faq.a: The command line runs on Windows and Linux on both Intel and ARM, and on Apple silicon Macs. The desktop window ships for Windows on Intel, Linux on Intel and Apple silicon Macs. Intel Macs are not supported and nothing is built for them.

faq.q: Do I have to install anything?
faq.a: No. Download the archive for your system, unpack it and run the binary. There is no installer, no runtime to add and no dependency to resolve. If you have Go, a single go install command works as well.

faq.q: Why is a run over thousands of files slower on Windows?
faq.a: Because Windows charges more for every path it looks at, and a command that goes over thousands of files looks at thousands of paths. Measured on one machine with 3000 files of 1 kB, verify takes about 0.9 seconds on Windows and about 0.2 seconds on Linux in a container. A shorter output path makes the Windows figure smaller, because every folder above the files is part of what gets looked at.

damages.append-junk: Writes random bytes after the end of the file and keeps exactly the size you asked for, the way a file with something stuck to its end arrives.
damages.truncate: Cuts the end off the file and keeps exactly the size you asked for, the way an interrupted upload or copy leaves it.
damages.zero-head: Overwrites the first bytes of the file with zeros, leaving its length alone. Most readers look there first, so this is the damage almost anything notices.

recipeKeys.allow_nondeterministic: Consent to formats whose bytes differ from run to run. Every format of this build repeats to the byte, so `true` is refused for now and the line can be left out.
recipeKeys.defaults: Settings every target takes unless it says otherwise.
recipeKeys.defaults.fill: How the content of the files is made. Not built yet: a recipe with this key is refused, and the content always comes from the seed.
recipeKeys.defaults.label: Whether each file carries a short label saying which run made it. `true` unless you say otherwise. The label is written so that the file stays valid.
recipeKeys.engine: The version of tfg the recipe needs. Not built yet: a recipe with this key is refused, and the manifest records the version that ran.
recipeKeys.extends: A preset to build on, written as `preset:size-boundaries`. Its files come first, and the targets of the recipe are added after them.
recipeKeys.locale: The language of the generated content. Only `en` is available, so any other value is refused, and the line can be left out.
recipeKeys.output.dir: The directory for the files and the manifest. A relative path is read from the directory you run in, not from the one the recipe is in. `--out` replaces it.
recipeKeys.output.manifest: The file name of the manifest. `manifest.json` unless you say otherwise.
recipeKeys.output.split_threshold: Splitting a large manifest into several files. Not built yet: a recipe with this key is refused, and the manifest is always one file.
recipeKeys.policy: Rules for settling the expectations that depend on your system. Not built yet: a recipe with this key is refused. Write `expected` on each target instead.
recipeKeys.seed: The number every byte of the run comes from. The same seed gives the same files on any machine. `0` unless you say otherwise.
recipeKeys.targets: The list of things to produce. Every target needs an `id`, a `format` and exactly one of `size`, `size-range`, `boundary` or `contains`.
recipeKeys.targets.boundary: Three files around a limit: one byte under it, the limit itself and one byte over it. Written as a size, such as `5mb`.
recipeKeys.targets.contains: For an archive: the files inside it, as a list of entries, each with a `format`, a `count` and a `size`.
recipeKeys.targets.count: How many files the target makes. `1` unless you say otherwise.
recipeKeys.targets.damage: Ways to break the files on purpose, applied in the order listed. Each one is a name, such as `zero-head`, or a `type` with its settings. `tfg damage` lists them.
recipeKeys.targets.expected: What your system should do with these files: `accept`, `reject`, `sanitize` or `unspecified`, alone or with a `reason`. The manifest carries it beside every file.
recipeKeys.targets.fill: How the content of these files is made. Not built yet: a recipe with this key is refused.
recipeKeys.targets.format: The format of the files, by its id, such as `pdf` or `png`. `tfg formats` lists them.
recipeKeys.targets.group: A name of your own for the kind of case these files are. The manifest carries it, so a report can group by it.
recipeKeys.targets.id: The name of the target. It is unique in the recipe, the seeds of its files come from it, and the manifest names it beside every file in `target_id`.
recipeKeys.targets.label: Whether these files carry the label. Overrides `defaults.label` for this target alone.
recipeKeys.targets.name: The template for the file names, such as `invoice_{index:04}.pdf`. `{index:04}` is the number of the file, four digits or more, and the only placeholder there is.
recipeKeys.targets.properties: The settings of the format, such as `pages` for a PDF or `width` and `height` for a picture. The page of format settings lists every one.
recipeKeys.targets.purpose: A sentence or two on what these files are and why they are in the set. The manifest carries it, and the instructions written beside the manifest are made from it.
recipeKeys.targets.send-as: The name to give these files to your system under, when it is one no disk stores, such as `../climbed_out.jpg`. The file keeps an ordinary name on disk, and the manifest carries this one in `send_as`.
recipeKeys.targets.size: The exact size of every file, such as `300kb`, `10mb` or a plain byte count. Units count in 1024s. `smallest` makes a picture as small as it can be at its `width` and `height`.
recipeKeys.targets.size-range: A size drawn for each file from a range, such as `1kb-8kb`. The draw comes from the seed, so the same seed gives the same sizes.
recipeKeys.version: The version of the recipe format. Required, and `1` in this build.
recipeKeys.with: The settings of the preset named in `extends`, written the way its flags take them, such as `limit: 5mb`. A setting left out takes its default, and the manifest says so.

manifestFields.manifest_version: The version of the manifest format, `1.0`. New fields are added without changing it, so a reader ignores the fields it does not know.
manifestFields.generated_at: When the manifest was written, in UTC.
manifestFields.tool.name: Always `testing-files-generator`.
manifestFields.tool.version: The version of tfg that made the files.
manifestFields.tool.go: The version of Go tfg was built with, so a hash that changed after an upgrade can be traced to it.
manifestFields.tool.generators: The version of the generator of each format the run used, by format. It moves when the bytes a generator writes change.
manifestFields.run: The settings that shaped this run.
manifestFields.run.seed: The seed of the run. The same seed and the same settings give the same files.
manifestFields.run.command: The command that started the run, as it was typed.
manifestFields.run.platform.os: The operating system, such as `windows`, `linux` or `darwin`.
manifestFields.run.platform.arch: The processor architecture, such as `amd64` or `arm64`.
manifestFields.run.complete: `false` when the run stopped early, for example after Ctrl+C. The manifest is written even then, so `cleanup` can remove what was made.
manifestFields.run.recipe_hash: The hash of the recipe in its settled shape, so reformatting the recipe keeps it. Present when the run came from a recipe.
manifestFields.run.overrides: The values a flag took over from the recipe, by name. Present when a flag replaced a value of the recipe.
manifestFields.run.overrides.*.from_flag: The value the flag gave, which the run used.
manifestFields.run.preset: The preset the run came from. Present only for a run of a preset.
manifestFields.run.preset.question: The question the preset answers.
manifestFields.run.preset.parameters: Every setting of the preset as the run used it, the ones you gave and its defaults together.
manifestFields.run.preset.defaulted: The settings you did not give, which took the default of the preset. A limit that came from a default is not the limit of your system.
manifestFields.run.instructions: The name of the file written beside the manifest that says in words what each file is and why it is in the set. Present when a file has a purpose.
manifestFields.summary: Counts over the whole run, for a quick check.
manifestFields.summary.file_count: How many entries the manifest has, one for each file the run planned.
manifestFields.summary.total_bytes: How many bytes the run wrote to disk, in all.
manifestFields.summary.materialized: How many files are on disk. Lower than `file_count` when a name could not be written or a file failed.
manifestFields.summary.by_format: How many files of each format.
manifestFields.summary.by_expected: How many files of each outcome.
manifestFields.summary.by_target: How many files each target made, by target id.
manifestFields.files: One entry for each file of the run.
manifestFields.files[].id: The handle of the file in this manifest, such as `f_0001`, numbered across the whole run.
manifestFields.files[].path: Where the file is, relative to the directory of the manifest. `verify` and `cleanup` find the file by this.
manifestFields.files[].name: The file name, the last part of `path`.
manifestFields.files[].send_as: The name to give the file to your system under, when the recipe asked for one no disk stores. Present only then.
manifestFields.files[].materialized: Whether the file is on disk. A name the system refused is still a test case, and still has its entry.
manifestFields.files[].target_id: The id of the target the file came from.
manifestFields.files[].bytes: The size of the file in bytes.
manifestFields.files[].fidelity: How faithful the file is to its format. `tfg formats` says it for each format.
manifestFields.files[].hashes.sha256: The SHA-256 of the file, which `verify` compares.
manifestFields.files[].seed: The seed this file was made from, which comes from the seed of the run and the id of the target.
manifestFields.files[].generator: The generator that made the file.
manifestFields.files[].generator.name: The name of the generator.
manifestFields.files[].determinism: Whether the same seed gives the same bytes, `byte`, or only the same size.
manifestFields.files[].properties: The settings of the format the file was made with, such as its width and height.
manifestFields.files[].expected: What your system should do with the file.
manifestFields.files[].expected.reason: The rule in play, from the closed list, such as `size_limit`.
manifestFields.files[].expected.confidence: `certain`, or `policy_dependent` when the right reaction depends on how your system is set up.
manifestFields.files[].expected.policy_options: The answers an outcome that depends on your system leaves open, for a test that settles it by your own policy.
manifestFields.files[].group: The group the recipe or the preset gave the file.
manifestFields.files[].purpose: What the file is and why it is in the set, in words.
manifestFields.files[].label_embedded: Whether the file carries the label that says which run made it.
manifestFields.files[].damage: What was broken on purpose, in the order it was done. Absent for a file nothing damaged.
manifestFields.files[].damage[].settings: Its settings as the run used them, the defaults included.
manifestFields.files[].damage[].cut: Where a cut fell in the file. Present for `truncate`.
manifestFields.files[].damage[].cut.in: What the first byte cut away was part of: `content`, `padding`, `structure` or `end`.
manifestFields.files[].damage[].cut.content_bytes: How long the content of the whole file was, where that is known.
manifestFields.files[].damage[].cut.content_kept_bytes: How much of the content is still in the file.
manifestFields.files[].notes: Things worth knowing about this file, such as a label that did not fit.
manifestFields.files[].notes[].code: A short code for the note, such as `cut_in_padding`.
manifestFields.files[].failed: `true` for a file the run could not make. The run carries on and ends with exit code `8`.
manifestFields.files[].error: Why the file could not be made.

image-upload.title: Image upload
image-upload.text: JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF around a 5 MB limit, one pixel and 36 megapixels, a corrupt JPEG, a PNG cut short, a PDF named as a photo and a name that climbs out of the folder.

media-upload.title: Video and sound upload
media-upload.text: MP4, WebM and WAV around a 10 MB limit, a portrait phone video, ten minutes of video, silence and a video cut short.

spreadsheet-import.title: Spreadsheet import
spreadsheet-import.text: One table as CSV with commas, semicolons and tabs, CRLF, no header and every field quoted, a wide and a large CSV, Excel sheets and two broken files.
